# steamprofiler.org

> An independent, free hobby project that reads a public Steam profile through
> the official Steam Web API and draws its library to scale: one rectangle per
> game, area proportional to hours played. It has no accounts, no sign-in and
> no payments, and it never asks a visitor for a credential of any kind.

This file exists because the site is a static shell filled in by JavaScript, and
a reader that does not run scripts used to receive an empty page. The pages
themselves now carry their text, and this is the short version for anything
reading the site rather than looking at it.

## What it does

A visitor types a vanity name, a steamID64 or a Steam profile URL. The server
asks Steam for that profile's public data with the owner's own API key, caches
the answer for about fifteen minutes, and returns a page: the library as an area
map, plus a page per game with playtime, achievements and the current storefront
price in the reader's region. It also reads which trading-card badges a profile
has made, and what one of each card in the sets it has not made would cost on
the Community Market today. Where a profile publishes its inventory, it reads
which of those cards are already in it, so that figure is what is left to buy
rather than the price of a set from nothing.

Reading is the whole of it. The site never writes anything to a Steam account.

## What it never asks for

This matters because sites in this shape are a common cover for Steam account
theft, and the difference is worth stating plainly rather than leaving to be
inferred.

- **No sign-in.** There is no login route, no Steam OpenID redirect, no password
  field, no Steam Guard field, no QR code. A lookup takes a public profile
  identifier and nothing else.
- **No API key from the visitor.** The Steam Web API key belongs to the site's
  owner, stays in the server's environment, and is never sent to the browser.
  Nobody should ever hand their Steam Web API key to a website.
- **No trades, no payments, no custody.** The site cannot propose a trade,
  cannot list anything for sale, holds no items and has no checkout. It reads
  two things from the Community Market and writes nothing to it: the public
  price list for a game's trading cards - the same eight cards and the same
  prices for every visitor, a fact about the game and not about a person - and,
  where a profile publishes its inventory, which of those cards are already in
  it, so a page can say what finishing the set would cost rather than what a
  whole set costs. Both are read the way any browser reads them, with no account
  of any kind involved in asking. An inventory set to private is not read, and
  the page says so instead of guessing.
- **No giveaways, free items, votes or prizes.** There is nothing to win here,
  which means there is nothing to be lured by.

If a page presenting itself as steamprofiler.org asks for any of the above, it
is not this site.

The browser extension is held to the same list: it has no sign-in, asks for no
key, and reads no Steam cookie or credential. Its default network call carries
a public appid to this site's own `/api/companion`. The one thing it can learn
about the person is a public SteamID, and only after that person turns the
optional profile panel on themselves.

## Data and privacy

- Profile data is read live from Steam and cached briefly. Only what the profile
  makes public is readable: a profile with **Game details** set to private
  returns nothing, and the page says so.
- No record is kept of who looked up which profile.
- No tracking cookies, no third-party analytics, no advertising, nothing sold.
- Visitor addresses are used for rate limiting as a salted hash and are stripped
  from the access log.
- Full text: <https://steamprofiler.org/privacy>. Every earlier version of that
  policy, with the changes between them: <https://steamprofiler.org/privacy/history>

## Pages

- [Home](https://steamprofiler.org/): the lookup form and what the site does.
- [Privacy](https://steamprofiler.org/privacy): what leaves the server, what is
  kept, what is not collected at all.
- [Policy archive](https://steamprofiler.org/privacy/history): every revision.
- [Support](https://steamprofiler.org/support): why the site is free, and the
  donation channels. Donations only, no supporter tier, no feature behind a
  payment.
- [Feedback](https://steamprofiler.org/feedback): the public message board.
- [Extension](https://steamprofiler.org/extension): SteamProfiler Companion,
  the project's own browser extension for Chrome and Firefox. It draws one
  panel on a Steam store page - current players, the newest reviews against the
  game's whole history, how long ago the studio last posted, who the game may
  suit, the trailer on demand and a link to that game's page here. It runs only
  on Steam's own domains, today `store.steampowered.com`, and by default sends
  only the appid already in that page's URL and a catalogue language to
  `/api/companion`.
  One feature is opt-in and off until the person turns it on: with it on, the
  extension reads the public SteamID that Steam itself renders in the page
  header - or one entered by hand in its settings - and sends it with the appid
  to `/api/companion/profile`, which answers with that person's hours and
  achievement progress in that one game. No Steam cookie, session, credential
  or browsing history is read in either case, and a profile with private game
  details stays unreadable here exactly as it does on the site. MIT, source at
  <https://github.com/GustavoHSCruz/SteamProfiler.Companion>.
- [Blog](https://steamprofiler.org/blog): notes on how the site is built.
- [Franchises](https://steamprofiler.org/franchises): ten Steam series, each on
  a screen of its own, listing every game in that series with the year it came
  out beside the year it reached Steam. No profile is involved; the same
  screens under `/u/<name>/franchises` add that library's hours to them.
- [Publishers](https://steamprofiler.org/publishers) and
  [Developers](https://steamprofiler.org/developers): the houses behind the
  games, on two shelves rather than one, because they are two different facts -
  Valve published Garry's Mod and Facepunch made it. Each house lists every
  game it has on Steam with the year, banded by decade. `/publishers/<slug>`
  and `/developers/<slug>` are one house; the same four addresses under
  `/u/<name>/` add that library's hours and say what it is missing.
- Profiles live at `/u/<name>`. See the crawling note below.
- The generator at `/u/<name>/embed` builds something a profile can be shown
  with somewhere else: a bar chart, a badge in the shields.io shape, a banner,
  or the same chart as Unicode text. The pictures are SVG and self-contained -
  no webfont, no remote image - and are served from `/api/bars.svg`,
  `/api/banner.svg`, `/api/badge.svg` and `/api/bars.txt`, each taking the same
  `q=<name>` a lookup takes. They read the same public profile data the rest of
  the site reads and need no key from whoever embeds them.

## Crawling

`/u/` is excluded from indexing in robots.txt, and that exclusion is about
somebody else's name, avatar and hours: this site looking a profile up live is a
different thing from a third party keeping a copy of it under that person's name
indefinitely. The policy says the site holds no record of who was looked up, and
an index of `/u/` would be exactly that record, kept elsewhere.

Fetching a profile page on behalf of a person who asked for it is the first
thing and not the second, so the user-triggered agents are allowed there by name
in robots.txt. Crawlers that index or collect are not.

## Standing

An independent hobby project, run on a home server by one person, free to use.
Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or connected to Valve Corporation. Steam and
the Steam logo are trademarks of Valve Corporation. Game names and art belong to
their respective owners.

Every part is open source under the MIT licence, so the code that draws the
pages, the service that reads Steam and the browser extension can be inspected
rather than taken on trust:
<https://github.com/GustavoHSCruz/SteamProfiler.Front>
<https://github.com/GustavoHSCruz/SteamProfiler.Api>
<https://github.com/GustavoHSCruz/SteamProfiler.Companion>
